original_question: Fix a prime power q and an integer r relatively prime to q-1. Determine how many elements x of the finite field F(q) satisfy the equation x^r + x = 1.
target_in_paper: Section 7.2 (Fixed points), Problem 18: determine the number of roots x in F(q) of x^r + x = 1, where q is a prime power and gcd(r,q−1)=1. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s formal target almost verbatim: it has the right ambient finite field F(q), the right arithmetic condition gcd(r,q−1)=1, and the exact equation x^r+x=1 from Problem 18. It also stays with the narrow counting problem actually stated in the paper, rather than drifting to the neighboring Welch fixed-point problem of Problem 19. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, it helps to state explicitly that F(q) denotes the finite field with q elements. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

In the nearby source context from Theorem 3, r arises via β=α^r for primitive roots α,β∈F(q)^*, so r is naturally understood modulo q−1; equivalently, one may take 1≤r≤q−2 with gcd(r,q−1)=1. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

The paper’s Problem 18 counts roots in all of F(q), not only in F(q)^* and not only among primitive elements. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

If the motivating equivalent formulation is mentioned, it should be stated as a fixed-point question for the G2 Golomb permutation from Theorem 3; in that interpretation the paper notes the correspondence 'excepting x=1'. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

There are no extra asymptotic, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency hypotheses here; the paper asks the exact counting problem for every prime power q and every admissible r. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
refined_question: Let q be a prime power, and let r be an integer taken modulo q−1 (equivalently, choose 1≤r≤q−2) with gcd(r,q−1)=1. Determine the number of solutions x∈F(q) to the equation x^r + x = 1. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, if q=p^m and α,β are primitive roots of F(q) with β=α^r, then for the G2 Golomb permutation f:[q−2]→[q−2] defined by α^{f(i)}+β^i=1, determine the number of fixed points i with f(i)=i; the paper identifies this with the number of roots of x^r+x=1 in F(q), phrased there with the fixed-point interpretation excluding x=1. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
justification: The draft is targeting Section 7.2, Problem 18, not a broader neighboring question. The nearby context explicitly derives Problem 18 from fixed points of G2 permutations by specializing Theorem 3 with β=α^r, which explains the coprimality condition gcd(r,q−1)=1. The next problem in the paper, Problem 19, concerns the different Welch/W1 fixed-point equation i ≡ Cα^i mod p arising from Theorem 1, so your draft should not be rewritten in that direction. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
